events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Arjun proposes Arjun, Kenji. I’ll join Kenji for the first mission; with no prior results, this gives us an initial team to assess.

I have concerns about this team. Arjun put himself on it for mission one with no results to go on, and I'm not comfortable sending him out without a clearer reason. Kenji, how do you feel about Arjun being on this team? I'd like your view before I vote.

Leo, it is standard for a leader to include themselves on Mission 1 since they know their own alignment. From my perspective, I know I am Good, so I can guarantee my own card, though I don't know Arjun's alignment yet. Arjun, what made you select me specifically for this first mission over Zara, Leo, or Elena?

Kenji, I chose you as an initial partner without any particular evidence against or in favor of the others. I included myself because I know my own alignment, and a two-person mission gives us a starting result to discuss. I understand Leo's concern, but there isn't a stronger evidence-based team available yet.

I'm not satisfied with Arjun's answer. He says he chose Kenji without evidence for or against anyone, and that he included himself because he knows his own alignment. That explains why he trusts himself, but it doesn't give the rest of us a reason to send him on a mission with no results. Kenji has given his own alignment, which is useful, but his statement also doesn't tell us anything about Arjun. I'm voting against this team. If we keep the same two-person structure, we should pick a team that doesn't put Arjun on the first mission without a reason, and players should explain their choices with specifics rather than general claims about standard practice.

Leo, I understand your objection, but the same lack of evidence applies to any first-mission team. Rejecting me simply because I included myself doesn't make an alternative more trustworthy. I favor keeping Arjun and Kenji so we can get a result to assess.

I've been following this discussion, and I think Leo's objection is weaker than he makes it sound. He says Arjun hasn't given us a reason to send him on a mission with no results — but no reason exists for anyone on Mission 1. That cuts equally against every possible team we could put forward. If we reject Arjun and Kenji on those grounds, we'll end up rejecting the next proposal and the one after that for exactly the same reason, and all we'll have accomplished is burning rejections before we have a single piece of information to work with.

Kenji already made the key point: leaders on the first mission routinely include themselves because it's the one card they can vouch for with certainty. Arjun paired that with Kenji, who has openly claimed his own alignment and asked a direct, reasonable question about the selection. Arjun answered that he had no evidence either way on anyone. That's an honest answer — in a five-player game with a two-person first mission, there simply isn't information to distinguish us yet.

What does bother me is the direction Leo is pushing. He's asking us to treat self-inclusion as inherently suspicious and to demand 'specifics' that cannot exist at this stage. That kind of standard doesn't help Good find Evil — it just creates noise and pressure to reshuffle teams based on nothing. If anything, I'd expect someone genuinely trying to get a read on the table to welcome getting a result on the board rather than blocking the first team over a concern that applies to every player equally.

I'm comfortable with Arjun and Kenji going. It gives us a mission result to reason from, it follows a sensible structure, and nothing Leo has raised actually distinguishes this pair from any alternative. I'd rather see the vote taken than have us keep relitigating a decision that has no better option available.

I'm voting against Arjun and Kenji. Arjun's answers confirm he picked Kenji and himself without any basis, and Kenji's reply only vouches for Kenji, not Arjun. Elena, you argue that rejecting this pair wastes a rejection because no team is better informed, but that doesn't explain why Arjun should be the one on the first mission. Being on the team is a choice the leader made without a reason. Elena, what specific reason do you have to believe Arjun should be on this mission rather than Zara or yourself? I'd like a direct answer before we vote.

Leo, you asked me directly for a specific reason to believe Arjun should be on this mission rather than Zara or myself, so here is my direct answer: I don't have one, and neither do you. That is precisely my point. I have no information that distinguishes any player at this table as more or less trustworthy for Mission 1, and you have presented none either. What you've presented is a demand for evidence that cannot exist before the first mission result, applied selectively to one player.

Let me walk through your actual objection. You say being on the team is a choice the leader made without a reason. But the leader is the only position at this table that comes with any structural legitimacy — Arjun was handed leadership by the game, and including himself is the one choice he can make with full knowledge of his own card. Asking him to justify his own inclusion over Zara or me is asking him to pretend he has reads he cannot have. His honest answer was that he had no evidence either way. You called that insufficient. By your standard, every leader on Mission 1 is insufficient, and we should burn rejections until Evil wins by attrition.

Notice what your position actually accomplishes. If we reject this team, the next leader faces the identical information vacuum. Either they propose an equally arbitrary pair — which you'll reject again for the same reason — or we cycle through five rejections and hand the game over without a single mission being run. A player genuinely trying to find Evil should want information on the board. A player benefitting from Good staying blind should want exactly what you're advocating: endless procedural objections that apply to everyone equally and therefore reveal nothing.

Kenji has vouched for his own card. Arjun has explained his reasoning and answered every question put to him directly, including yours. Nobody at this table has offered a single concrete read against him — not you, not anyone. Your case rests entirely on the absence of a reason that no alternative team would have either.

So my position is straightforward: I support Arjun and Kenji. It gets us a result, it follows the standard structure, and rejecting it trades a mission outcome for pure noise. Arjun, the vote is coming and Leo has now pressed the same objection three times without offering an alternative team or any distinguishing evidence. If you keep the team as proposed, are you prepared to stand by that choice through the vote, or do you see any value in a revision that would only trade one arbitrary pair for another and reward the standard Leo is setting?

Elena, I’m standing by Arjun and Kenji. A revision would be equally speculative at this stage, and the proposed team gives us a starting result to assess. Leo is free to vote against it, but I don’t think his objection gives us a stronger alternative.

I’m Zara. I’ve listened to the exchange around Arjun and Kenji. On Mission 1, I do not have any concrete evidence for or against Arjun or Kenji, and I don’t think anyone at this table has a real read yet. Leo’s concern about Arjun’s self-inclusion is understandable, but it does not distinguish this pair from any other possible two-person team: every Mission 1 proposal would be based on the same lack of public information. Elena’s point that rejecting this team would only replace one arbitrary pair with another is persuasive to me. Kenji has spoken clearly about his own alignment, and Arjun has answered the questions put to him directly. I do not have a specific reason to oppose either of them, and I would rather get a mission result on the board than spend rejections on a standard that no team can satisfy at this stage. I support approving Arjun and Kenji so we have actual information to assess next.
Arjun confirms Arjun, Kenji. I’m keeping Arjun and Kenji as proposed; the discussion gave me no compelling reason to revise the team.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).

Zara proposes Zara, Leo, Elena. Mission 1 failed with Arjun and Kenji, so at least one of them is Evil. As Zara, I know I am Good, so I propose the three players not on that failed team: Zara, Leo, and Elena.

I need everyone to listen carefully to the math of this game. I am Good, and I submitted a Success card on Mission 1. Since Mission 1 received a Fail card, Arjun is 100% guaranteed to be Evil. There is no ambiguity about this from my perspective.

In a five-player game, there are exactly three Good players and two Evil players. Since Arjun is Evil, the other Evil player is exactly one of Zara, Leo, or Elena, meaning the other two are Good. 

That leads to a critical conclusion: any team of three that excludes me—such as the currently proposed team of Zara, Leo, and Elena—is mathematically guaranteed to contain the second Evil player and fail. The only way Good can succeed on Mission 2 is by putting together all three Good players: me and the two Good players among Zara, Leo, and Elena.

Zara, assuming you are Good as you claim, your current proposal is walking straight into a failure because it has to contain that second Evil player. Understanding that Arjun is Evil and I am Good, which of Leo or Elena do you find more trustworthy to join the two of us?

Kenji, you asked me to say which of Leo or Elena I find more trustworthy. I do not have private evidence that lets me rank them, and I will not pretend otherwise. My proposal is Zara, Leo, and Elena because I know my own card is Good, and I want to test the failed Mission 1 pair from outside that team. Your argument that Arjun is 100% Evil depends on the table trusting your claim that you submitted Success. Publicly, Mission 1 only establishes that at least one of Arjun and Kenji is Evil; it does not clear Kenji. The stronger and more self-serving claim is that the only successful Mission 2 team must include Kenji himself. That is exactly what an Evil player from the failed team would say to stay on the next mission. Between Leo and Elena, Leo raised a consistent concern about Arjun's self-inclusion, though I disagreed with blocking the first team over it. Elena argued forcefully for approving the failed team, which is a point I am weighing. I do not have enough to name one as more trustworthy. I support Zara, Leo, and Elena because it avoids both members of the failed team and gives us a cleaner read.

Zara, I'm not comfortable with Elena on this team. In the Mission 1 discussion, Elena pushed hardest to approve Arjun and Kenji after Leo's objections, and she argued that rejecting the pair would waste rejections, even though the rest of the table was still deciding. She also reacted strongly to Leo's concerns instead of simply asking for more information. Kenji is the one member of the failed pair who has made a clear, checkable claim about his own card, and he has been consistent about it. Zara, would you consider revising the team to Kenji, Zara, and Leo? That keeps the team to players who have stated their own Success intent and avoids the seat that Elena's pattern makes risky. Please respond to that specific suggestion before the vote.

Leo, I’ve considered your suggestion to revise to Kenji, Zara, and Leo. I’m not going to do that. Mission 1 failed with Arjun and Kenji; publicly that means at least one of them is Evil, and it does not clear Kenji. Kenji’s claim that he submitted Success and that Arjun is 100% Evil is exactly the claim a member of the failed team would make to stay on Mission 2. Replacing Elena with Kenji would put one of the two unresolved failed-team seats onto this mission and weaken the cleaner test of Zara, Leo, and Elena. Your concern about Elena is noted: she argued strongly for the first team, and that is a fair point to weigh. But a strong argument for a team that later failed is not the same as evidence that Elena is Evil; Good players can argue for a bad team on Mission 1. The current proposal excludes both Arjun and Kenji, includes me, and gives us a result from three players outside the failed pair. I prefer that to trading Elena for Kenji on the basis of Kenji’s self-vouching. I’ll vote to approve Zara, Leo, and Elena as proposed.

Zara, I'm not comfortable sending Elena on this mission. In Mission 1 she argued hardest to approve Arjun and Kenji, pushed back on every concern I raised, and that team failed. Publicly, that pattern is a real reason to keep her off a team that has to succeed. Kenji has made a specific claim about his own card, and I'd rather test that claim than take Elena's word. Zara, will you revise the team to Kenji, Zara, and Leo? If you won't, I'll vote against Zara, Leo, and Elena, because I don't think this team is safe enough to send out.

Leo, you asked whether I will revise to Kenji, Zara, and Leo. No. Mission 1 failed with Arjun and Kenji, so publicly at least one of them is Evil; it does not clear Kenji. Kenji’s claim that he submitted Success and that Arjun is 100% Evil is exactly the claim a member of the failed team could make to stay on Mission 2. Replacing Elena with Kenji would put one of the two unresolved failed-team seats back on this mission and weaken the cleaner test of Zara, Leo, and Elena. I agree Elena argued strongly for the first team, but a Good player can argue for a bad team on Mission 1. That is a point to weigh, not proof she is Evil. Your concern about Elena is noted, but your proposed alternative asks the table to trust Kenji’s self-vouching more than the public failure of his team. I will keep Zara, Leo, and Elena. Leo, if your objection is that Elena’s Mission 1 support for Arjun and Kenji is a real risk, what distinguishes that from Kenji’s actual presence on the failed team and his self-serving claim that only a team including him can succeed?

Zara, thank you for answering directly. I'm going to vote against Zara, Leo, and Elena, and I want to be specific about why. What distinguishes Elena from Kenji is the pattern of behavior, not a claim I can prove. On Mission 1, Elena pushed harder than anyone to approve Arjun and Kenji, dismissed every objection as noise, and called rejecting the pair a waste. When that team failed, she did not ask what had gone wrong or revisit her position. Kenji's claim about his own card has been stated plainly and consistently, and no one has presented a concrete contradiction to it. Zara, you say a strong argument for a bad team is not proof of Evil. I agree. But Good players do not need proof to avoid a seat that carries this much risk on a mission that must succeed. Kenji, Zara, and Leo is a team of three players whose statements have been consistent, and it is the safer option. Elena, I asked you earlier to explain why you pushed so hard on Arjun and Kenji after the objections were raised. I'd like your direct answer before the vote: do you still believe the Mission 1 team was the right call, and what would you have done differently knowing it failed?

Leo, you asked me directly whether I still believe the Mission 1 team was the right call and what I would do differently. Here is my answer: yes, at the time, approving Arjun and Kenji was the correct decision with the information available. Every player at this table agreed there was no evidence distinguishing any pair before a result existed. The fact that the mission failed does not retroactively make approval wrong — it makes it informative, which is exactly what I said it would be. What would I do differently? Nothing about the reasoning; I would simply now update on the result, which is what I am doing. And Leo, notice that your own record cuts both ways: you voted against the first team, but you also spent that entire discussion objecting on grounds that applied to every possible team equally. Being on the right side of one coin flip is not a read. Now to the substance of this proposal. Leo, your case for swapping me out for Kenji rests entirely on one thing: Kenji's private claim that he submitted a Success card. That claim is unverifiable, and it comes from a member of the team that just failed. Look at how convenient Kenji's story is. He vouches only for himself, pins the entire failure on Arjun, declares Arjun one hundred percent Evil based on evidence only he can see, and then concludes that every viable Mission 2 team must include Kenji himself. That is precisely the position a Evil player on the failed team would take: stay clean, stay on the next mission, and let the table do the work of clearing him. Publicly, Mission 1 tells us at least one of Arjun and Kenji is Evil. It does not tell us which. If Kenji is the Evil one, then his entire speech in this discussion is exactly what we would expect to hear, word for word. I am not asking anyone to conclude Kenji is Evil. I am asking the table to recognize the asymmetry: my alleged sin is that I argued for a team that any informed player could have supported, while Kenji's alleged innocence rests on a claim only he can verify, made by a player who needs that claim to be believed in order to stay on missions. Those are not equivalent risks. A team of Zara, Leo, and Elena excludes both members of the failed pair, includes Zara who knows her own card, and produces a clean result that actually tests something. Leo's alternative tests nothing except Kenji's willingness to repeat his own story. Kenji, I will put one question to you directly, since you have spoken with great confidence about what the table should believe: you say you played Success and that Arjun is Evil, which would mean the second Evil player is one of Zara, Leo, or me. Beyond your own unverifiable card claim, what actual evidence do you have against any one of the three of us — anything

Elena, you asked what evidence exists against any of the three of you beyond my knowledge of my own card. Here is the evidence on the table for everyone to see.

First, look at Leo’s record on Mission 1. Leo was the lone vote against Arjun and me. If Leo were Evil alongside Arjun, he would have had zero reason to cast the sole, glaring rejection against his own partner on a mission Evil was positioned to fail. His suspicion of Arjun proved entirely correct.

Second, look at your own record, Elena. You spent two extensive speeches in Mission 1 running interference for Arjun, dismissing Leo's legitimate concerns as baseless noise, and aggressively pushing the table to approve an Evil leader's proposal. Now that Arjun has failed the mission, you dismiss that defense as merely 'informative' and turn all your energy toward ensuring that the three players outside Mission 1—which mathematically must contain the second Evil player—go together.

To Zara and Leo: I know you cannot privately verify my card, but think about the incentives. An Evil player who just failed Mission 1 does not loudly insist on the exact mathematical reality that Good must unify to win. An Evil player in Elena's seat, however, desperately wants Zara, Leo, and Elena approved, because that guarantees Evil is on the team without having to fight for it.

Elena, answer this directly: if you are Good and genuinely trying to deduce alignments, why do you treat your aggressive defense of an Evil player as harmless, while treating Leo—the only person who correctly opposed that Evil player—as a liability?

Kenji yielded to me, so I'll answer his question directly: why do I treat my defense of the Mission 1 team as harmless while treating Leo as a liability? Because I don't treat Leo's Mission 1 vote as a liability at all — Leo was entitled to it, and being on the right side of that result is to his credit. What I treat as a liability is Leo's current proposal, and I want the table to see exactly what it rests on.

Kenji's entire case is a chain that begins and ends with his own private claim. Strip out "I played Success" and every conclusion collapses. He says any three-person team excluding him mathematically must contain Evil — but that is only mathematics if his card claim is true. There is a fully consistent alternative: both members of the failed team are Evil, one played Fail and one played Success to bank credibility. In that world, Kenji's speech in this discussion is word-for-word the play you'd expect — claim Success, pin the failure on your teammate, declare yourself mathematically indispensable, and engineer your way onto every future mission. Kenji says an Evil player on the failed team wouldn't loudly insist on the math. Wrong: an Evil player who played Success on Mission 1 would insist on nothing else, because that insistence is his ticket onto Mission 2.

And notice the asymmetry Kenji keeps glossing over. He demands that I be swapped out based on public behavior — arguing for a team everyone could have supported with zero information. He wants himself inserted based on a claim only he can verify, made by a member of the team that just failed, on a mission that must succeed. Leo, think about what you'd actually be trading: the seat you suspect, based on things we can all see, for a seat that requires us to take Kenji's word as mathematics.

The proposal in front of us needs nobody's private claim. It excludes both members of the failed team, includes Zara, who knows her own card, and produces a clean result that genuinely splits the table's uncertainty. Kenji's alternative tests nothing except his willingness to repeat his own story. I'm voting to approve Zara, Leo, and Elena, and I'd urge everyone who wants real information on the board to do the same rather than hand a must-win mission to the one narrative we cannot check.

Look closely at the story Elena is now forced to sell: she actually suggested that Arjun and I could both be Evil, with one failing and one succeeding to bank credibility. 

Think about how absurd that is. In a five-player game, there are exactly two Evil players. If both Evil players were on Mission 1, Evil would have completely thrown the game on round one! If both of us were Evil, then Zara, Leo, and Elena would be guaranteed Good, and you three could simply vote yourselves onto Missions 2, 3, and 4 for an effortless Good sweep. Evil would never hand Good an automatic win by putting 100% of their team on Mission 1.

That leaves the only reality: exactly one of Arjun and me is Evil. Mission 1 failed, which means the second Evil player is sitting among Zara, Leo, and Elena. That is an inescapable mathematical fact. Therefore, any team composed of Zara, Leo, and Elena is guaranteed to contain that second Evil player and will fail.

Elena is inventing impossible scenarios because she is that second Evil player, and she knows that if Zara, Leo, and Elena are sent, Evil wins another mission without lifting a finger. 

Leo already sees this clearly and has stated he will vote against this proposal. Zara, sending this team guarantees a second failure and puts Good on the brink of defeat. I am voting Reject on Zara, Leo, and Elena, and anyone who wants Good to have a path to victory must vote Reject as well.

Kenji’s certainty goes beyond what the public result establishes. One Fail card means at least one of us is Evil, not that exactly one is. He cannot rule out both of us being Evil simply by arguing that it would be a bad strategy.

I support Zara, Leo, and Elena. The proposal excludes both players from the failed mission and gives us a result from a different group. Kenji’s claim that this team is guaranteed to fail depends on accepting his own account of Mission 1 as fact.

Kenji's latest argument deserves a direct answer, because he is now asking this table to treat his reasoning as mathematics when it is nothing of the sort.

He says the scenario where both members of the failed team are Evil is 'absurd' because Evil would never put both of its players on Mission 1. But look at what actually happened: Arjun was the leader, and Arjun chose the pair. If both were Evil, that would have been a blunder by the Evil side — and blunders exist. More importantly, 'Evil would never' is a prediction about strategy, not a fact about cards. Kenji is asking you to convert an assumption about how Evil ought to play into certainty about who is Evil. That is the same move he has made all discussion: begin with his private, unverifiable claim, and end with a conclusion that happens to require the table to put him on every future mission.

Notice also what Kenji's argument demands from you. He wants you to reject Zara, Leo, and Elena — a team that excludes both members of the failed pair and includes Zara, who knows her own card — based entirely on his word that he played Success. He offers you no checkable evidence. His case against me rests on my having argued for a team that every player at this table, including Zara, acknowledged was defensible before any result existed. Arguing well for a team that later failed is not Evil; it is exactly what an uninformed Good player does on Mission 1.

And consider the information value of the vote in front of us. Kenji has staked his entire position on the claim that Zara, Leo, and Elena is guaranteed to fail. If that is true, rejecting costs nothing. But if this team is approved and succeeds, Kenji's story collapses — his 'mathematical fact' would be exposed as a fabrication, and we would know the failed pair's surviving member lied. Approving this team is the single fastest way to test the one narrative at this table that nobody can currently verify. Rejecting it protects that narrative indefinitely and burns this mission on Kenji's say-so.

Leo, I know you've raised your concerns sincerely, and you were right to be suspicious before the first result. But the alternative you're backing requires trusting the self-serving claim of a player from the failed team over a clean test that excludes that team entirely. Arjun has also pointed out the same flaw: one Fail card establishes that at least one of the failed pair is Evil, not exactly one, and Kenji cannot close that gap by asserting his own card.

I'm voting to approve Zara, Leo, and Elena. It excludes both members of the failed mission, it can be evaluated without accepting anyone's private claims, and it produces a result that either advances Good or exposes the loudest voice demanding we avoid it.

Zara confirms Zara, Leo, Elena. I am keeping Zara, Leo, and Elena. Mission 1 failed with Arjun and Kenji, so publicly at least one of them is Evil; this proposal excludes both and gives a clean result without relying on Kenji's unverifiable claim that only a team including him can succeed.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Leo proposes Zara, Leo. I'm proposing Zara and myself. Mission 2 succeeded with Zara, Leo, and Elena, and Zara has been consistent and clear. Arjun and Elena are the Evil players I can see, so I'm keeping both off this team. A two-person team of Zara and me gives us a strong chance to succeed.

Mission 2 succeeded, but a Success card does not prove everyone on it is Good: Evil can play Success. Leo now says he can see that Elena and I are Evil, yet he proposes Zara and himself while excluding Elena, who was also on the successful team.

I would prefer Zara and Elena: they both supported the successful Mission 2 team, while Leo opposed it. His certainty about Elena deserves scrutiny, especially since her mission succeeded.

Leo, the successful Mission 2 team included Elena, yet you now say you can see that she is Evil. That certainty deserves an explanation; the public result does not establish it. I would prefer Zara and Elena, who both supported the successful team, over a pair that includes Leo, who opposed it.

Zara, how do you weigh Leo’s opposition to the successful team against his new claim about Elena?

Arjun asked me how I weigh Leo’s opposition to Mission 2 against his new claim about Elena. I weigh it heavily. Leo voted against the only team that has produced a Success, and now he wants to exclude Elena from that successful team while inserting himself alongside me. Mission 2 succeeding does not prove Elena is Good, since an Evil player can play Success, but it also does not support Leo’s assertion that he can “see” Elena is Evil. That claim goes beyond the public result, and it is especially concerning because Leo opposed the team that succeeded.

I know my own card is Good. The proposed team is Zara and Leo. Whether I can support it depends entirely on whether Leo is Good, and his public record does not give me confidence: he rejected both the failed Mission 1 team and the successful Mission 2 team, and his current rationale relies on certainty the rest of us cannot check. I am not comfortable approving a must-succeed mission that includes Leo unless he explains why his opposition to the successful team should be trusted and what public evidence distinguishes Elena from any other player. Leo, what specific public evidence supports your claim that Elena is Evil, and why should the table trust you on this mission after you voted against the team that just succeeded?

Zara, fair challenge. I can't prove Elena's alignment publicly, so here is the record I'm weighing. On Mission 1, Elena was the strongest voice pushing the Arjun and Kenji team through. When I objected, she called my concerns noise and said rejecting the pair was wasteful, and she kept pressing that point. On Mission 2 she again argued hard for her own seat. Mission 2 succeeding doesn't clear her, because an Evil player on a successful team can simply play Success. My vote against Zara, Leo, Elena was about her pattern, not about protecting Kenji. I accept that Mission 2 succeeded, and I'm not calling you anything but Good. My proposal is Zara and me, which keeps Elena and Arjun off a mission that has to succeed. Arjun has also pushed to keep the failed team together and has asked for Zara and Elena, so the pairing he prefers is one the table should be careful about. Zara, what would you need to see from me to approve Zara and Leo?

Leo, you asked what I need to approve Zara and Leo. I know my own card is Good, so the decision is whether the table can trust you on a must-succeed mission. I do not have public proof that Elena is Evil; your case is a pattern read, and it sits alongside your vote against the only successful team, Zara, Leo, and Elena. Mission 2 succeeding does not clear Elena, but it also does not support the certainty you stated. Arjun and Kenji remain unresolved from the failed Mission 1, and I will not treat your unverified read about Elena as stronger than the public results. Leo, will you revise to Zara and Elena, the pair from the successful Mission 2 team, rather than excluding Elena on an unverified read? If you will not, explain what public evidence distinguishes Elena from you beyond your own assertion.

Zara, you asked for public evidence that Elena is Evil. Here is the record I can point to without claiming more than I can back. On Mission 1, Elena was the most forceful defender of Arjun and Kenji. She called every objection noise, said rejecting the pair was wasteful, and kept pressing the vote after the leader's self-inclusion had already been challenged. On Mission 2, she again argued for her own seat, and in her later speeches she shifted attention to Kenji's claim while the leader of the failed team, Arjun, went largely unexamined. Arjun has since endorsed Elena's team and now asks you to pair with her. Mission 2 succeeding does not clear Elena, since Evil can play Success, and I am not claiming it does. I am asking you to weigh her pattern of advocacy on the one team that failed. On Arjun's proposal of Zara and Elena: he is pairing you with the player whose Mission 1 advocacy I have described, and that pair excludes anyone who questioned the first team. That is not a neutral choice. To approve Zara and Leo, I can only offer my public record: I voted against the failed team and against the team that later succeeded, and I stated my reasons for each at the time. I am not asking you to trust me beyond that record. If you want a different partner, name the public evidence that clears Elena and I will consider it.

Leo has clarified that his case against Elena is a pattern read, not public proof. But he is asking us to exclude someone from the successful Mission 2 team while relying on that same success for his choice of Zara. His opposition to that team also deserves weight, even if he explained it at the time.

I favor Zara and Elena. Both supported the team that succeeded, and both were on it. That result does not clear either of them, but I see less reason to replace Elena with Leo based on his unverified suspicion.

Zara, given Leo's explanation, do you still prefer Zara and Elena, and will you reject Zara and Leo if he keeps it?

Arjun, yes: I still prefer Zara and Elena, and I will vote against Zara and Leo if Leo keeps this proposal. My reason is public: Mission 2 succeeded with Zara, Leo, and Elena. That does not prove Elena is Good, since Evil can play Success, but it is the only positive mission result we have. Leo's case against Elena is a pattern read he admits is not public proof, and he voted against the team that produced that success. Replacing Elena with Leo asks me to trust Leo's unverified suspicion over the result and over Elena's participation in it. I know my own card is Good; the question is whether Leo gives me a safer partner than Elena. So far he has not. Leo, will you revise the team to Zara and Elena? If you keep Zara and Leo, I will reject it. If you revise to Zara and Elena, I will consider approving that pair, because it preserves the successful Mission 2 pairing and avoids putting a player who opposed that success onto a must-succeed mission without checkable evidence.

Zara, thank you for pressing me. I can't prove Elena's alignment from public information, and I'm not claiming Mission 2's success clears her, since Evil can play Success. My concern is her public pattern. On Mission 1 she was the most forceful voice for Arjun and Kenji, called every objection noise, and said rejecting the pair was wasteful. On Mission 2 she argued for her own seat. Since then she has moved attention to Kenji's claim while Arjun, the leader of the team that failed, has gone largely unexamined. Arjun has now endorsed Elena and asked you to pair with her. I'm asking you to weigh that pattern, not a secret. I'm also not accusing Kenji. One Fail card only tells us at least one of the failed pair is Evil, so I'm not treating his card claim as proof either way. The proposal of Zara and Leo excludes both Arjun and Elena from a mission that has to succeed, and it doesn't rely on anyone's unverifiable claim beyond our own cards. Zara, what public action by Elena would move you toward trusting her, one that doesn't rest on her Mission 2 card?

rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
